concept_note_requirements.req: Build and evaluate a virtual environment in which a knowledge domain's structure and relationships are translated into spatial organisation and explored through movement and interaction.
refs: a virtual environment in which the structure and relationships within a knowledge domain are deliberately translated into spatial organisation and explored through movement and interaction

concept_note_requirements.req: The contribution to deliver and evidence is the knowledge-to-space transformation method and its measured cognitive consequences, not 3D museum technology.
refs: The proposed contribution is not the 3D museum technology itself. It lies in the knowledge-to-space transformation method and in measuring its cognitive consequences.

concept_note_requirements.req: Implement the five-stage pipeline: classify the domain, model its relationships, transform them into spatial architecture, let users navigate it, and measure reconstruction afterwards.
refs: Classify a heterogeneous knowledge domain → model its internal relationships → transform those relationships into spatial architecture → allow users to navigate that architecture → measure whether users reconstruct the domain differently afterwards
Epistemic classification → relational modelling → spatial transformation → guided situated exploration → epistemic reconfiguration

concept_note_requirements.req: The study must answer RQ1–RQ3: relational understanding versus an informationally equivalent interface; acquisition, transfer and cognitive load; and navigation pathways in relation to the constructed knowledge structures.
refs: Does an epistemically spatialised craft-learning environment produce stronger relational understanding than an informationally equivalent conventional interface?
How does epistemic spatialisation affect knowledge acquisition, transfer and cognitive load compared with conventional information navigation?
How do users' navigation and interaction pathways within the immersive environment relate to the knowledge structures they construct after learning?

concept_note_requirements.req: Test the primary hypothesis: greater improvement in relational knowledge structure for the spatialised environment than for the conventional structured interface.
refs: users of the epistemically spatialised environment will show greater improvement in relational knowledge structure than users receiving the same knowledge through a conventional structured interface

concept_note_requirements.req: The database may hold all six block-printing traditions; the experimental prototype should use three traditions of comparable information depth.
refs: the full database may retain all six traditions, but the experimental prototype should probably use three carefully selected traditions with comparable information depth

concept_note_requirements.req: Organise every selected tradition with a common epistemic template: context; materials and tools; process sequence; artisan decisions and tacit knowledge; design and material outcomes; scientific and technological explanations; comparison with other traditions.
refs: Each selected tradition can be organised using a common epistemic template

concept_note_requirements.req: The scientific layer answers concise causal 'why' questions about pretreatments, mordants and materials, reactions, process order, and environmental and water conditions.
refs: The scientific layer will answer concise causal questions such as why a pretreatment is necessary, why a particular mordant or material is used, why X and Y produce Z, why process order matters, and why environmental or water conditions change outcomes.

concept_note_requirements.req: Provide a well-designed 2D web interface with the same text, images, artisan and process information, science, comparisons and learning prompts, navigated by menus, cards, headings and hyperlinks.
refs: A well-designed 2D web interface containing the same text, images, artisan/process information, scientific explanations, comparison content and learning prompts. Users navigate through menus, cards, headings and hyperlinks.

concept_note_requirements.req: Present the same information transformed spatially: rooms as learning spaces, objects as entry points, and relationships expressed through adjacency, sequence, proximity, pathways and progressive disclosure.
refs: Rooms become learning spaces, objects become entry points into knowledge, and meaningful relationships are represented through adjacency, sequence, proximity, pathways and progressive disclosure.

concept_note_requirements.req: Simplify the museum for the experiment: remove social and live functions and unnecessary controls, minimise the map, hide instructions after onboarding, and disclose information progressively.
refs: Social/live functions and unnecessary controls should be removed; the map may be minimised; interface instructions should disappear after onboarding; and information should be progressively disclosed.

concept_note_requirements.req: The two pathways must be informationally equivalent and differ primarily in spatial organisation.
refs: two informationally equivalent knowledge pathways that differ primarily in spatial organisation

concept_note_requirements.req: Target about 40 participants in a between-group design of about 20 per pathway; a counterbalanced within-participant design with matched traditions is an alternative, to be decided later.
refs: A simple between-group design can allocate approximately 20 participants to each pathway.
The final choice can be made after the prototype content has been prepared. To be decided later.

concept_note_requirements.req: Procedure: short prior-knowledge test, assigned learning task, immediate post-test, relational reconstruction task, and a short UX and cognitive-load questionnaire.
refs: All participants complete a short prior-knowledge test, the assigned learning/exploration task, an immediate post-test, a relational reconstruction task, and a short UX/cognitive-load questionnaire.

concept_note_requirements.req: Measure relational understanding before and after learning by having participants organise and connect a fixed concept set.
refs: Before and after learning, participants can organise or connect a fixed set of concepts such as material, fibre, mordant, dye, water, block, process sequence, environmental condition, reaction and colour outcome.

concept_note_requirements.req: Concept-map measures: valid relations, incorrect relations, causal-chain depth, structural similarity to an expert reference map, and increase in cross-category relations.
refs: Possible measures include number of valid relations, incorrect relations, depth of causal chains, structural similarity to an expert reference map, and increase in cross-category relationships.

concept_note_requirements.req: Measure knowledge acquisition (pre and post), transfer to a new 'why?' problem, validated perceived cognitive load separating content difficulty from interface burden, accuracy and completion time, short UX (SUS, UMUX-Lite or UEQ-S), and presence as a brief supplementary measure.
refs: Knowledge acquisition: pre/post factual and conceptual questions.
Transfer: ability to solve a new 'why?' problem not directly encountered in the interface.
Cognitive load: short validated perceived-load measure, with attention to separating content difficulty from interface/navigation burden.
Task performance: accuracy and completion time.
Usability/UX: a short measure such as SUS, UMUX-Lite or UEQ-S.
Presence/engagement: a brief supplementary measure rather than the central outcome.

concept_note_requirements.req: Log behaviour automatically in the immersive prototype, and mirror the same logging in the 2D interface where possible.
refs: The immersive prototype should log user behaviour automatically. The same logging logic should be mirrored where possible in the conventional interface.

concept_note_requirements.req: Events to log: room/page entered, entry and exit timestamps, exhibit/object selected, information layer opened, artisan/process/science layer selected, query asked, sequence of interactions, return to earlier object/room, cross-tradition movement, guidance cue used, abandoned or incorrect pathway, task completion time, unique concepts encountered, repeated concepts/links.

Derive path length, exploration breadth and depth, revisit rate, cross-domain transitions, science-layer engagement, path entropy and sequence patterns; compare navigation structure with the post-learning concept map.
refs: Derived indicators may include path length, exploration breadth, exploration depth, revisit rate, cross-domain transitions, science-layer engagement, path entropy and sequence patterns.
A particularly interesting analysis would compare a participant's navigation structure with the concept map produced after learning.

concept_note_requirements.req: Lightweight guidance (signalling, self-explanation) should stabilise attention while preserving agency; the guidance approach (e.g. exploration first, guidance when required) is an open decision.

Suggests a hybrid design: exploration first, guidance when required. (interesting – we may have to take a call on what approach we will use)

concept_note_requirements.req: Keep interface complexity, navigation and choice from adding extraneous load; distinguish content difficulty from interface and navigation burden (a potential confound).
refs: interface complexity, navigation and excessive choice may introduce extraneous cognitive load
Reinforces the need to distinguish content difficulty from interface and navigation burden. (Can become confounding variables)

concept_note_requirements.req: Eight-week plan: week 1 freeze RQs, traditions, schema and instruments; weeks 1–3 content and immersive prototype; week 3 2D interface and logging; week 4 expert validation and a pilot with about 5–6 users; weeks 5–6 main study; weeks 6–8 analysis and writing.

Section 3.1 says the authors gathered 737 sentences (the line break splits 'senten-ces') describing 191 exhibits from 10 online exhibitions. The abstract calls them '737 exhibit commentary descriptions', so 'exhibit commentaries' suggests 737 separate commentaries when the data cover only 191 exhibits. The paper is also internally inconsistent: the per-exhibition counts in Table 2 (PDF p. 5) add up to 178, not 191 (20+28+18+9+13+20+27+12+17+14), and Appendix A (PDF p. 21) gives 32 ceramics and 28 Egyptian exhibits where Table 2 gives 20 and 27. The taxonomy itself is supported: 5 main categories and 40 sub-themes. 'Links knowledge types to XR delivery' is only partly supported. The links come from interviews with 16 curators (§5) and the authors' design implications (§6). No XR docent was built or tested, and the authors say curator wishes may not match what learners need. The paper is about exhibit commentary in art and history exhibitions, which is narrower than a 'museum knowledge taxonomy'.

quotes.quote: This research suggests that learning in IVR leads to higher extraneous CL than learning in less immersive media, and highlights the importance of considering CL when designing IVR learning tools.
If instructional support and learning processes are not emphasized, even the latest technological advancements may have limited instructive value.
level of prior experience with IVR is an important external factor to control for

cn_characterisation_checks.note: The paragraph has no citation, but its claims match CAMIL: IVR raises extraneous load, and effects depend on instructional method rather than the medium. The specific mechanisms 'navigate space' and 'learn unfamiliar controls' are not stated as load sources in CAMIL. Controls and navigation appear only as usability and prior-experience external factors (PDF pp. 15-17). 'Knowledge organisation' is not discussed.

requirements.requirement: Measure presence and agency as the core psychological affordances (process variables) in both pathways, not only an overall engagement score. If presence is measured, decide explicitly which of CAMIL's three dimensions (physical, social, self-presence) applies; physical presence is the relevant one for a museum without social actors.

quotes.quote: The general affordances of learning in IVR are presence and agency.
the CAMIL distinguishes between three different dimensions of presence including physical, social, and self-presence

requirements.requirement: Where the questionnaire budget allows, include measures of the CAMIL mediators (situational interest, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, embodiment, cognitive load, self-regulation) and the external factors. CAMIL itself names no instrument in its text; its reference list cites the Multimodal Presence Scale (Makransky, Lilleholt & Aaby 2017) as a presence measure.

quotes.quote: we hope that researchers will include measures of the variables included in the CAMIL, as well as the external factors, when conducting research on the use of IVR for learning.
Development and validation of the multimodal presence scale for virtual reality environments

requirements.requirement: Build the knowledge tests on an explicit knowledge taxonomy that scores factual, conceptual and (if applicable) procedural knowledge and transfer separately, instead of a single declarative score. Concept-map relational items count as conceptual knowledge ('classifications and categories, principles ..., models, and structures').

quotes.quote: Future research should use knowledge taxonomies to differentiate between different learning outcomes
Conceptual knowledge can include classifications and categories, principles and generalizations, and theories, models, and structures.
The types of learning outcomes predicted by the CAMIL include factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge, and transfer of knowledge

requirements.requirement: Do not expect the spatial/immersive pathway to beat the 2D pathway on factual recall. Pre-register factual items as a secondary outcome where a null or reversed effect is plausible, and keep the primary hypothesis on relational/conceptual structure.

quotes.quote: These results suggest that IVR is not necessarily the ideal medium for teaching factual knowledge

Parong and Mayer (2018) found that an immersive VR lesson was less effective than a PowerPoint lesson for acquiring factual knowledge, but they found no significant difference in conceptual knowledge acquisition.

requirements.requirement: Design the transfer task ('why?' problem) so it is not situated in a specific room or object of the museum. The test must require applying the knowledge outside the spatial context in which it was learned, and the risk of context-bound learning should be reported.

quotes.quote: immersive lessons are also typically situated, which could make it difficult to transfer knowledge to a different situation.

requirements.requirement: Minimise extraneous load from searching the 3D scene. Relevant knowledge objects must be easy to find in the field of view, and seductive or decorative details that do not carry knowledge must be removed or visually subordinated.

quotes.quote: this can also increase extraneous cognitive load because learners have to find relevant content, specifically when the content includes seductive details that are not necessary for learning

more complex visual representations and details, which represent better representational fidelity and can lead to higher presence, may also lead to virtual environments that result in higher extraneous CL and less learning.

requirements.requirement: Constrain choice in the spatial pathway: offer bounded, meaningful options (e.g. ordered rooms, progressive disclosure) rather than unrestricted autonomy over what to view and interact with. Agency raises extraneous load and does not automatically increase learning.

quotes.quote: Similarly, more agency does not necessarily mean more learning when it can lead to more extraneous CL.

which allowed for more agency by giving learners autonomy to view the content of their choices and to interact with features in an interactive immersive laboratory simulation, was not optimal or conducive to learning because this might have led to extraneous CL

requirements.requirement: Apply the coherence principle. Remove material and functions that invite hedonic, non-instructional activity (social/live features, unnecessary controls, decorative interactions) from both experimental pathways.

quotes.quote: the coherence principle (Mayer and Fiorella 2014; e.g., leave out irrelevant material that leads to hedonic activities but does not support learning)

Hedonic information systems focus on the fun aspect of using the system and are designed to provide self-fulfilling rather than instrumental value to the user, thereby encouraging prolonged rather than productive use.

requirements.requirement: Signal relevant features (e.g. highlighting the knowledge object or relation currently relevant) without breaking presence: use diegetic or in-world cues rather than intrusive overlay panels where possible.

quotes.quote: the signaling principle (Mayer and Fiorella 2014; e.g., help learners focus their attention on relevant features in a way that does not diminish their presence)

requirements.requirement: Manage essential processing. Provide pre-training (onboarding to controls and key concepts) and learner-paced segments (progressive disclosure per room/layer). Decide whether to use the modality principle (spoken instead of printed words), applied identically in both pathways to preserve informational equivalence.

quotes.quote: including the pre-training (Meyer et al. 2019), segmentation (present multimedia messages in learner-paced segments; Parong and Mayer 2018), or modality principles (use spoken rather than printed words in a multimedia message

requirements.requirement: Build explicit reflection/self-explanation checkpoints into or immediately after the exploration, e.g. a summarising or explaining prompt after each room or segment. Without them, highly engaging environments can undermine self-regulated learning.

quotes.quote: introducing reflection activities that prompt metacognition and deeper learning within, or after, IVR is critical
self-regulated learning can suffer when immersive lessons do not provide natural reflection opportunities

Reflection activities can take the shape of explaining the content of a lesson to an avatar peer in VR, or to a real peer after an IVR lesson (Klingenberg et al. 2020), or summarizing after segments of an IVR lesson

requirements.requirement: Measure prior knowledge before exposure and use it as a covariate or moderator. CAMIL argues that learners without prior knowledge may experience presence and agency as entertainment without integrating the information.

quotes.quote: having high prior knowledge enables the affordances of presence and agency to be conducive to learning by allowing learners to interpret their experiences in the IVR lesson in a meaningful way.

learners who have no prior knowledge to anchor these experiences on may experience entertainment value stemming from high presence and agency, without properly selecting, organizing, and integrating the information into long term memory.

requirements.requirement: Frame and design the comparison as a test of an instructional method (epistemic spatialisation) rather than a media comparison. Hold immersion level, control factors and representational fidelity as constant as possible across pathways, or measure them, so that a difference cannot be attributed to the medium.

quotes.quote: Rather than conducting media comparisons that could potentially lead to a body of research that may not show any consistent differences between modalities
This view prioritizes research which investigates interactions between media and instructional methods.

requirements.conflict_note: Qualification, not outright contradiction. Concept note P91: 'The intended comparison is therefore not a 'fancy 3D museum' versus a plain webpage, but two informationally equivalent knowledge pathways that differ primarily in spatial organisation.' Yet Pathway A is 'A well-designed 2D web interface' navigated by 'menus, cards, headings and hyperlinks' (P88) and Pathway B is the 3D Hand Block Museum (P90). These differ in medium (3D navigable environment vs 2D web), control factors and representational fidelity as well as in spatial organisation. CAMIL argues that such media comparisons may show no consistent differences and that effects come from method x media interactions. The design therefore confounds spatial organisation with medium unless the confound is controlled or measured.

requirements.requirement: Record each participant's prior experience with VR/3D environments and games, and control for it (covariate or stratification). Novelty effects inflate effort and attention only transiently.

quotes.quote: level of prior experience with IVR is an important external factor to control for
the effect of novelty is only transient and may never take the place of instructional support.
Prior experience and familiarity with IVR is also an essential factor to consider as this makes it possible to investigate novelty effects.

requirements.requirement: Measure usability and screen for cybersickness, spatial ability and working memory as external factors. Fix navigation errors found in the pilot, because low usability (e.g. errors in navigating) breaks presence and reduces agency.

quotes.quote: These encompass usability, social factors, and a range of individual differences variables, including age, tendency to experience cyber sickness, working memory, personality, predisposition towards absorption, and spatial ability.
Low usability, e.g., by virtue of errors in navigating, may also result in breaks in presence. Likewise, low usability may impair the users' sense of agency through limiting their control.
Cyber sickness is also a factor known to occur for some users of HMDs (Munafo et al. 2017), and can diminish learning from IVR by shifting the learners' focus.

requirements.requirement: To raise presence and agency, the spatial pathway should provide smooth view changes (stable high frame rate, no stutter), a realistic but uncluttered display, and a high degree and immediacy of control (low input latency). Record the display type (HMD vs desktop) as a fixed study parameter.

quotes.quote: designing the environment for use with an HMD, ensuring a realistic display of the environment and smoothness of view changes, and affording a high degree and immediacy of control.
Control factors encompass variables such as degree of control, immediacy of control, and mode of control

requirements.requirement: When citing CAMIL for a desktop or web-based 3D museum, state that CAMIL's paths are theorised for HMD-based IVR and that desktop 3D is 'low immersion' in its terms. Do not claim that CAMIL predictions apply unchanged unless an HMD is used.

quotes.quote: in this paper, we focus on immersive learning experiences that are accessed through an HMD (which we refer to as IVR)
Simulations or 3D worlds accessed through a desktop computer or tablet are referred to as low immersion or desktop VR in the literature and will only be used as comparisons to IVR in this paper.

requirements.requirement: Make bodily and navigational actions meaningful for the learning outcome. Movement between rooms or objects, and manipulation of objects, should correspond to the knowledge relation being learned (e.g. walking a process sequence), not be arbitrary travel.

quotes.quote: there is evidence that learning increases when bodily interactions and visual features of a particular concept are coordinated
That is, when physical activities are meaningful for the learning outcome, such as manipulating an object to understand its physical dimensions.

requirements.requirement: Give learners real control over their actions and environment parameters (choose what to open, where to go). A fixed, non-interactive narrative tour yields low agency, so guidance should not collapse exploration into a fixed narrative.

quotes.quote: low agency would result from immersive virtual environments where interaction is not possible and where the user follows a fixed narrative.

control factors (positive relation, path 3 in Fig. 2; e.g., being able to control the body representation and modify the environment and its objects) are regarded as the most important predictor of agency in the CAMIL.

requirements.requirement: Do not interpret long dwell times or extensive exploration in the logs as learning by default. Analyse them against outcome measures, because engaging environments can produce 'prolonged rather than productive use'. Log information-seeking events (layer opens, queries) as behavioural correlates of situational interest.

quotes.quote: Hedonic information systems focus on the fun aspect of using the system and are designed to provide self-fulfilling rather than instrumental value to the user, thereby encouraging prolonged rather than productive use.
Situational interest may elicit short-term, situational knowledge-seeking behavior

requirements.requirement: Design for the dual goal stated by CAMIL: reduce unnecessary (extraneous) processing caused by interface and navigation while keeping cognitive engagement high. Cognitive-load measurement must therefore separate extraneous load from content-related load.

quotes.quote: The goal of instructional design is to optimize learning by reducing the degree of unnecessary processing (extraneous CL) produced by the learning task, while simultaneously increasing cognitive engagement
extraneous CL negatively influences the learning of factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge, as well as the transfer of this knowledge

requirements.requirement: Treat CAMIL paths as hypotheses, not established effects, when using them to justify design choices or interpret results. The authors state that the model is largely untested.

quotes.quote: few empirical studies have specifically tested the paths outlined in the model.

cn_characterisation_checks.cn_text: Petersen, Petkakis & Makransky (2022) | Shows how immersion and interactivity influence VR learning through presence and agency.

quotes.quote: Consistent with the predictions, both interactivity and immersion were shown to impact agency, physical presence, and embodied learning positively.
Hence, while interactivity and immersion did not directly affect learning, as mentioned above, there was evidence for indirect links.
Support for two indirect paths from VR features to learning was found: one involving situational interest and the other involving embodied learning.
Agency only predicted embodied learning
elevated levels of embodied learning decreased knowledge acquisition, presumably because of the lack of congruency between bodily actions and learning content.

cn_characterisation_checks.note: Immersion and interactivity did raise physical presence and agency. However, the routes to learning were indirect and not simply 'through presence and agency'. The positive route ran presence -> situational interest -> learning. Agency's only route ran through embodied learning, which predicted learning NEGATIVELY. There was no direct effect of immersion or interactivity on learning (no significant ANOVA effects on learning; PDF p. 10). 'Learning' here is declarative knowledge gain only.

cn_characterisation_checks.cn_text: Demonstrates that extraneous load can undermine the benefits of immersion.

quotes.quote: There was no significant effect of immersion on extraneous cognitive load environment.
There were also no significant effects on extraneous cognitive load interaction although the main effect of interactivity was close (p = .059).
it was in the opposite direction than predicted: Lower interactivity was associated with higher extraneous cognitive load environment.
cognitive load was found to predict the experience of presence, not the other way around as suggested by the theory.
difficulties with the interaction technique led to breaks in presence by leading the participants' attention towards the technological setup instead of the virtual learning content

cn_characterisation_checks.note: The study does not show extraneous load undermining the benefits of immersion on learning. Immersion had no effect on either extraneous-load subscale. Neither subscale predicted learning (predictions 18 and 19 were not supported; only predictions 14 and 16 were, PDF p. 11). Immersion produced no learning benefit to undermine (PDF p. 10). The closest finding is narrower and exploratory: extraneous load from the interaction technique was associated with lower physical presence (a SEM path added via modification indices), which the authors interpret as breaks in presence. They also found that LOWER interactivity raised environment-related extraneous load. The concept-note sentence should be rewritten, e.g.: 'interaction-related extraneous load was associated with reduced physical presence'.

requirements.requirement: Avoid an unanalysable media comparison. Either isolate the manipulated feature (here, spatial organisation) while holding immersion and interactivity constant across pathways, or cross the factors as Petersen et al. did (2 x 2: immersion x interactivity). At minimum, document which of immersion, interactivity and spatial organisation differ between Pathway A and B.

quotes.quote: VR studies often involve media comparisons that make it difficult to disentangle the relative effects of technological features on learning.
video (low immersion/low interactivity), PC (low immersion/high interactivity), VR-video (high immersion/low interactivity), and VR (high immersion/high interactivity).

requirements.conflict_note: Qualification. Concept note P91 says the two pathways 'differ primarily in spatial organisation', but Pathway A is 'A well-designed 2D web interface' with 'menus, cards, headings and hyperlinks' (P88) and Pathway B is a navigable 3D museum (P90). Under Petersen et al.'s definitions they also differ in immersion and in the kind of interactivity (teleport/walk-and-trigger vs hyperlink navigation). Petersen et al. warn that such comparisons make it difficult to disentangle which feature caused an effect.

requirements.requirement: Run and report an a-priori or sensitivity power analysis (e.g. G*Power, power 0.80, alpha .05). For reference, Petersen et al.'s 153 participants in four cells (~38 per cell) could detect only effects of f = 0.23 or larger (medium); a 2-group design with ~20 per group (concept note P94) will detect only substantially larger effects, so report the minimum detectable effect.

quotes.quote: With a power level of 0.80, a sensitivity analysis conducted using the G*Power software (Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, & Buchner, 2007) suggested that the study design amounted to

With a power level of 0.80, a sensitivity analysis conducted using the G*Power software (Faul, Erdfelder, Lang, & Buchner, 2007) suggested that the study design amounted to minimum detectable effects of f = 0.23 (p2 = 0.05) for main and interaction effects.
quotes.quote_fragment_original: detectable effects of f = 0.23

quotes.quote: Participants were then randomly allocated to one of four different conditions: VR (39), VR-video (39), PC (40), or video (35).

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Randomly allocate participants to pathways after consent. Keep participants blind to the existence of other conditions (separate rooms/sessions), and forbid note-taking and talking between participants during exposure.

quotes.quote: This made students blind to the fact that there were different conditions.
Participants were not allowed to take notes or interact with each other during the experiment.

requirements.requirement: A virtual museum is an established, validated format for declarative learning studies. Petersen et al. built a Unity 2020 exhibition hall toured in sequence (introduction, then three topic sections), with narration, virtual screens showing visuals, ambient sound and animated 3D models. The platform can follow this pattern (rooms = topic sections, exhibits trigger presentations).

quotes.quote: A virtual museum exhibition about viruses was developed in Unity 2020 and used as learning material.
Virtual screens were positioned around the exhibition hall to supplement the narrations with appropriate visuals during each presentation
The museum format was chosen due to its natural connection with providing declarative knowledge (the object of study)

requirements.requirement: Define 'interactivity' operationally and identically in documentation: high interactivity = learner controls pace and order (teleport/walk freely and initiate exhibit presentations); low interactivity = watching a pre-recorded optimal tour. Object pick-up was not part of the manipulation.

quotes.quote: In the first version, users were able to teleport around the museum and actively initiate the exhibition presentations (that is, a high level of interactivity was provided).
whereby the learner controls the pace and/or order of a learning episode.
It was not possible to pick up artefacts in the interactive version: Learners could walk around and instigate presentations (as in many real-life museums).

requirements.requirement: Record and report the exact hardware per condition (headset model and input device, or laptop and mouse, and audio via headphones), since the device defines the immersion level.

quotes.quote: For the VR condition (high immersion/high interactivity), Oculus Quest headsets with controllers were employed.
For the PC condition (low immersion/high interactivity), Dell Latitude 7490 laptops with a computer mouse were used.
Participants used headphones in the PC, VR and VR-video conditions.

requirements.requirement: Log time-on-task automatically in every condition. Petersen et al. could not report exposure time for the free-exploration groups, which left time-on-task uncontrolled between self-paced and fixed-length conditions.

quotes.quote: The video recording of an optimal run through the application was 10 minutes long.
We do not have data for the VR and PC groups, but they spent approximately ten to 15 min in the virtual environment due to being able to explore the environment freely.

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: To separate interface/navigation burden from other load, use the multidimensional cognitive load scale for virtual environments (Andersen & Makransky 2021). Its extraneous-load subscales are 'interaction' (4 items, e.g. 'The interaction technique used in the simulation was very unclear') and 'environment' (4 items), on a five-point Likert scale. Adapt wording ('simulation') for the 2D pathway.

quotes.quote: The extraneous cognitive load interaction scale consisted of four items from Andersen and Makransky (2021; e.g., The interaction technique used in the simulation was very unclear).
The extraneous cognitive load environment scale consisted of four items from Andersen and Makransky (2021; e.g., The elements in the virtual environment made the learning very unclear).
The validation and further development of a multidimensional cognitive load scale for virtual environments.
all items used in this study, except knowledge items, were measured on a five-point Likert scale.

requirements.requirement: Pilot the cognitive-load items before relying on them. Petersen et al. dropped the navigation-relevant items: 'difficult to master' (interaction) and 'difficult to find the relevant learning information' (environment, factor loading 0.58). Navigation/way-finding burden may therefore need its own validated item or behavioural indicator, such as logged abandoned paths.

quotes.quote: one item was shown during confirmatory factor analysis to have a low standardized factor loading (0.58;
It was difficult to find the relevant learning information in the virtual environment.
The interaction technique used in the simulation was difficult to master.

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: If presence and agency are measured (concept note P106), use the short scales Petersen et al. used: physical presence (5 items, Multimodal Presence Scale, Makransky, Lilleholt & Aaby 2017) and agency (3 items adapted from the Sense of Agency Rating Scale, SOARS, Polito, Barnier & Woody 2013). Both showed high reliability (alpha 0.89 and 0.90).

quotes.quote: The agency scale consisted of three items adapted from Polito, Barnier, and Woody (2013; e.g., During the lesson, my experiences and actions were under my control).
The physical presence scale consisted of five items from Makransky, Lilleholt, and Aaby (2017; e.g., The virtual environment seemed real to me).
Developing the Sense of Agency Rating Scale (SOARS): An empirical measure of agency disruption in hypnosis.
Development and validation of the multimodal presence scale for virtual reality environments

requirements.requirement: Measure situational interest (6 items, Knogler et al. 2015) as the engagement measure. In Petersen et al. it was the variable that carried the positive path from presence to learning. Optional affective scales: intrinsic motivation (5 items adapted from Makransky & Petersen 2019), self-efficacy (4 items adapted from Meyer et al. 2019 and the MSLQ, Pintrich et al. 1991) and embodied learning (3 items, Skulmowski & Rey 2018).

quotes.quote: The situational interest scale consisted of six items from Knogler et al. (2015;
The intrinsic motivation scale consisted of five items adapted from Makransky and Petersen (2019;
The self-efficacy scale consisted of four items adapted from Meyer et al. (2019) and Pintrich, Smith, Garcia, and McKeachie (1991;
The embodied learning scale consisted of three items based on Skulmowski and Rey (2018;
learning was positively predicted by the degree of situational interest experienced by the participants.

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Build the knowledge test from the content actually presented, with expert review (Petersen et al.: 9 four-option multiple-choice declarative items). Evaluate it edumetrically (average pre-to-post item increase; Petersen et al. retained items with increases over 0.2). Add conceptual and transfer items, since a purely declarative test cannot capture relational understanding.

quotes.quote: The knowledge test was based on the narration used during the virtual lesson and consisted of nine multiple choice questions with four possible answers
All knowledge items assessed declarative memory (Ten Berge & Van Hezewijk, 1999)
The knowledge test was edumetric, meaning that it was designed to measure the knowledge gain of individuals
The results indicated that all items had average pre-to post-test increases over 0.2 on a possible range of - 1 to 1.

requirements.requirement: Report scale reliability (Cronbach's alpha; 0.80-0.90 = very good per DeVellis 2012), and handle missing data by FIML or an equivalent principled method. Validate the questionnaire data-capture pipeline end-to-end before the main study: Petersen et al. lost 21 participants' self-efficacy scores to a measurement error.

quotes.quote: alpha levels between 0.80 and 0.90 were considered indicative of very good scale reliability.
maximum likelihood approach was used to deal with missing values (this was true for the self-efficacy scores of 21 participants due to a measurement error).

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Check group equivalence at baseline (demographics with chi-square/Fisher's exact tests; pre-test scales with one-way ANOVA) and report it. Analyse outcomes with factorial ANOVA (two-way for a crossed design) and report effect sizes (Cohen's d for simple effects).

quotes.quote: Fisher's exact test were conducted to assess the equivalence of conditions on demographic variables.
One-way ANOVAs were therefore performed to verify equivalence of conditions on these measures.
the effect of interactivity on agency is larger when immersion is low (d = 2.08) compared to high (d = 0.71).

requirements.requirement: If the spatial pathway runs on desktop (low immersion), self-directed navigation and active triggering of exhibits are especially important for agency and the sense of embodied learning. Do not replace it with an automated tour, because interactivity's effect on agency was largest under low immersion (d = 2.08 vs 0.71).

quotes.quote: having a high level of interactivity is more important for achieving a sense of agency and embodied learning when the lesson has a low level of immersion.
the effect of interactivity on agency is larger when immersion is low (d = 2.08) compared to high (d = 0.71).

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Do not assume that free exploration adds extraneous load. In Petersen et al., free exploration (high interactivity) produced LOWER environment-related extraneous load than passively watching an optimal tour, and immersion had no effect on either extraneous-load subscale. The study should test, not presuppose, that spatial navigation adds burden.

quotes.quote: Surprisingly, lower interactivity was associated with higher extraneous cognitive load stemming from the environment;
This finding goes against Moreno and Mayer's (2007) notion that free exploration of complex multimodal environments could generate heavy cognitive load.
There was no significant effect of immersion on extraneous cognitive load environment.

requirements.conflict_note: Concept note P5: 'Immersion can also increase cognitive load when users must simultaneously understand content, navigate space and learn unfamiliar controls.' P14: 'interface complexity, navigation and excessive choice may introduce extraneous cognitive load.' P32 attributes to this paper that it 'Demonstrates that extraneous load can undermine the benefits of immersion.' Petersen et al.'s data show no immersion effect on extraneous load, and the opposite direction for interactivity (passive viewing raised environment-related extraneous load). This qualifies the concept note's assumptions and contradicts its characterisation of this paper.
requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Keep the interaction technique (locomotion, selection, layer opening) simple and learnable, and include onboarding practice. Extraneous load from the interaction technique was associated with reduced physical presence, interpreted as attention shifting to the technical setup.

quotes.quote: physical presence was negatively influenced by extraneous cognitive load stemming from the interaction
difficulties with the interaction technique led to breaks in presence by leading the participants' attention towards the technological setup instead of the virtual learning content

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Plan for a possible null effect on knowledge gain. Petersen et al. found no main or interaction effect of immersion or interactivity on declarative learning, and the low-immersion/low-interactivity video group had the highest mean gain. The paper's contribution should not depend solely on a knowledge-gain difference (cf. concept note P161 on mixed results).

quotes.quote: Finally, the analysis did not reveal any significant effects on learning. Thus, hypothesis 9 was not confirmed.

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Make navigation and bodily actions structurally or analogically related to the knowledge content (e.g. moving along a process sequence, adjacency encoding causal links). When actions were unrelated to declarative content, the sense of embodied learning predicted learning negatively.

quotes.quote: Lindgren and Johnson-Glenberg (2013) contend that for effective learning to take place, actions must be structurally or analogically related to the learning content.

In the present study, it was not possible to perform actions explicitly related to the learning content, which is why the experience of actively using one's body for learning might have done more harm than good.
It should be noted that embodied learning impacted knowledge gain negatively contrary to what was expected

requirements.evidence_strength: finding from this study's own data

requirements.requirement: Avoid an identical pre- and post-test, or control for testing effects. A pre-test can direct attention to what the learner does not know and inflate post-test scores. This applies to the concept note's identical before/after concept-mapping task and its pre/post knowledge questions. Use parallel forms, or a post-only control or Solomon-type check if feasible.

quotes.quote: A pre-test may, for instance, direct attention towards what the learner does not know during subsequent instruction, thereby enhancing performance on the post-test (Hartley, 1973).

requirements.conflict_note: Concept note P98: 'Before and after learning, participants can organise or connect a fixed set of concepts', and P101: 'pre/post factual and conceptual questions.' Petersen et al. list re-use of the same knowledge test pre and post as a limitation (testing/sensitisation effect). Re-using the same fixed concept set before and after carries the same risk, and it applies to both pathways but may interact with the condition.

requirements.requirement: Measure, or at least screen, individual differences that may moderate effects: cybersickness, spatial ability and personality. Petersen et al. omitted them to keep the questionnaire short and flag this as a gap. Keep the total questionnaire short, but include spatial ability for a spatial-organisation manipulation.

quotes.quote: These include factors such as cybersickness, spatial ability, or personality traits (Makransky & Petersen, 2021).
the questionnaire length as short as possible, participants' ratings on such traits were not assessed.

requirements.requirement: Include signalling (highlighting essential material) and generative prompts (e.g. elaboration/self-explanation prompts), which the authors recommend as the next instructional techniques to test in VR museum-style lessons. Hold them constant across pathways so that they do not confound the spatial comparison.

quotes.quote: the signaling principle (i.e., highlighting essential material) could enhance the process of learning by reducing extraneous cognitive load (Mayer, 2014a).

quotes.quote: The results must provide sufficient data for calculation of effect size (ES) of an intervention, including means and standard deviations and errors (SD and SE),
Borenstein et al. (2009) suggested that Hedges' g can reduce the small-sample size bias.

requirements.requirement: Any coded data (e.g. concept-map relation scoring, query categories) must be coded by two independent trained coders with Cohen's kappa reported per code, disagreements resolved by discussion.

quotes.quote: Two trained coders independently performed all of the coding.

Cohen's k was 0.96 for museum type, 0.98 for learner type, 0.96 for learning domain, 0.98 for learning content, 0.90 for design element, and 0.96 for technology device. All disagreements were resolved through further discussion. 2.6.
quotes.quote_fragment_original: All disagreements were resolved through further discussion.

requirements.requirement: The immersive pathway should use interaction beyond overlaid labels (object manipulation/inspection, user-generated responses), since most AR/VR museum designs only superimpose label-like information and few let visitors interact with exhibits.

quotes.quote: This could be seen as a similar function of labels used for traditional exhibits.
However, only a few studies have explored applying AR and VR to enhance visitors' interactions with exhibits or allow visitors to generate virtual content in immersive environments

requirements.requirement: The scientific layer (e.g. why a mordant fixes dye) may be supported by dynamic visualisation of otherwise invisible mechanisms; if used in Pathway B, an equivalent visualisation must be available in Pathway A (see ZHOU-R02).

quotes.quote: AR can visualize the invisible mechanisms that underlie complex phenomena (Yoon et al., 2017).
Eight studies used these technologies to provide simulations or dynamic visualization of typically invisible phenomena

requirements.requirement: Report the delivery device and immersion level of each condition using an explicit device category (mobile, HMD, desktop, projector). If Pathway B runs on a desktop display, describe it as a desktop (low-immersion) virtual environment and do not claim HMD-level presence.

quotes.quote: allowed users to experience a high degree of immersion and provided a complete sense of presence.
Instead of merely providing animation on desktop devices with low immersion, the learning settings should make more use of VR technologies.

requirements.requirement: Provide hands-on device/interface training for all participants before the learning task, as in controlled AR museum studies, so control-skill differences do not contaminate learning outcomes.

quotes.quote: All of the participants received hands-on training on how to use the mobile AR app and were randomly assigned to experimental or control groups.
The experiment was conducted with 101 participants (from the general public) for 90 min in an anonymous national museum.

requirements.requirement: Pre-register that a null or negative result is possible and interpretable: individual AR/VR museum effects range from negative to large, and AR games have failed to beat pen-and-paper methods.

quotes.quote: Savela et al. (2020) found that AR games in a science center did not necessarily improve learning performance or social interaction when compared to the traditional pen-and-paper learning method.
The individual effect sizes of the 12 primary studies ranged from - 0.21 to 2.19.

requirements.requirement: Ground the immersive pathway's design rationale in experiential, situated, active and multimedia learning theory, and design for active meaning-making (learners searching for information) rather than passive viewing.

quotes.quote: The theoretical foundation of incorporating VR and AR in museum learning is grounded in experiential learning (Behrendt & Franklin, 2014; Kolb, 2014), situated learning (Falk & Dierking, 2000; Johnson, 2002), active learning (Prince, 2004), and the multimedia learning theory
Learners can be actively involved in cognitive processing when a coherent mental representation of their own experiences is constructed (Mayer, 2014).
